Gun lobbyists are gaining unprecedented sway in the union movement and the Socialist Left of the Victorian Labor Party, with insiders saying they are threatening delegates, dictating policy and inciting violence.

Before her appearance later this month at Melbourne Magistrates’ Court, where she is applying for intervention orders against a senior Victorian Labor Party figure and a union delegate, Helen Breier explains that she never wanted to go public.

“This is my Labor Party,” she says. “I joined Young Labor in 1975. The Labor Party is my team … but Victoria is in danger.”

Personally, she adds: “I’m scared.”

Obtaining no resolution of her complaints to both the state’s ombudsman and the Independent Broad-based Anti-corruption Commission (IBAC), she says she’s speaking out after exhausting internal efforts to thwart a “dangerous infection” within government.

“The gun lobby’s power over Victorian Labor is out of control,” says Breier, who has a finance career and is an elected member of Labor’s Conservation, Environment and Resources Policy Committee, among other senior party positions.

Breier alleges in her court applications that a senior Victorian Labor figure “used a video from an undisclosed source to threaten, intimidate and silence me” at the behest of hunting proponents. She also alleges an Australian Manufacturing Workers’ Union official, “a promoter and supporter of gun interests”, used intimidating methods to block her environment protection motions, and allowed a group of AMWU delegates to “harass and intimidate me”.

Breier and other delegates echo academic researchers who characterise Victoria’s government as having been “captured” by gun proponents who have cultivated influence within unions, secured senior bureaucratic positions and weakened gun-related laws incrementally since 1996, when the Howard government launched its gun buyback and other reforms. Back in 2018, University of Melbourne political researcher George Rennie wrote that gun lobbyists had since sought to “coopt democratic norms to force change, even when it is directly at odds with overwhelming public opinion”.

“I will be attacked for coming out of the tent, but I am being slaughtered inside the tent. I never signed up to the Shooters and Fishers Party, which is what Victorian Labor has become.”

One Labor delegate, who requested anonymity, says gun lobbyists “made inroads into certain Victorian trade unions”, which then “militantly demanded government recognition as stakeholders in environmental decision-making”, securing “a winding back of hard-won environmental protections, and ever greater access to the Victorian natural environment, including national parks”.

Through the AMWU, the Electrical Trades Union and the Construction, Forestry and Maritime Employees Union, gun proponents have formed delegate voting blocs within Labor’s dominant Socialist Left faction, amassing majority numbers to “dictate policy”, says Breier. These delegates allegedly threaten, intimidate, dox and humiliate those who resist their motions.

Another delegate tells The Saturday Paper that unions “strong-armed the Victorian government under the pretext of defending workers’ recreational rights, even though they cannot demonstrate what proportion of their memberships actually hunt”. The source says these unions “coercively ensured the continuation of native waterbird hunting”, despite a parliamentary inquiry recommending a ban in 2023.

“Any policy that is seen to limit gun use is blocked,” says Breier, who adds that she’s not against target or pest shooting but says she was nonetheless “warned” that gun lobbyists “were out to get” her. “Last year there was a threat to expel me from the party by someone I’d never met. Gun lobby interests have permeated all gun-related, and sometimes unrelated, policy.”

The “Building Industry Group” – a consortium of four major trade unions – campaigned against a ban on duck hunting, threatening to halt state infrastructure projects, including the Metro Tunnel, and bar Labor MPs from worksites if the government went ahead with it. The group also reportedly undermined the proposed Great Forest National Park, plans for which the government abandoned last year.

Gun and hunting exhibits now appear at union and Labor state conferences and Victoria’s parliament hosts the Responsible Shooting Expo. Unions have mounted campaigns normalising guns, with newspaper ads portraying hunters as emblems of freedom and masculinity. During proposed native duck shooting bans, one ad was headlined “Outdoor Recreation is under Attack!!”

Delegates say gun lobbyists have realised their dreams in the planned state “super-agency” Outdoor Recreation Victoria, ostensibly an environmental regulatory body that the government says will “initially focus on getting more Victorians out fishing, game hunting, boating, four-wheel driving and off grid camping”. This grouping of shooting alongside other recreation, says one insider, is designed to secure social licence and put voters off the gun-advocacy scent.

According to Breier’s IBAC complaints, key figures in environment agencies have links to shooting associations and shooters have family links with staff in senior party and government roles. One named is within the Game Management Authority (GMA), an agency whose “advocacy and promotional roles … conflict with its responsibilities as a regulator”, according to a 2017 state-commissioned review. And while wildlife rescuers seeking to document unlawful hunting were charged, the review also found there were failures to prosecute hunters.

During hunting season GMA’s Facebook page continues to host photos of rescuers – mostly women – and their hometown locations. The Saturday Paper has seen a letter sent to Victorian ministers, dated June 6, from “an alliance of women across Victoria who have reported threats and violence” allegedly committed by officers of the GMA and other state environment agencies. It lists “accounts, witnesses and documentation of victims” who endured “threats and abuse” from public servants and officers, amounting to “strong cases for misfeasance in public office”.

Researchers have identified weapons manufacturer Beretta and firearms importer and munitions manufacturer NIOA as being among the forces behind lobbyists, including the Shooting Industry Foundation of Australia (SIFA). And the Sporting Shooters Association of Australia (SSAA) boasts “a long friendship and affiliation” with America’s National Rifle Association. According to research from The Australia Institute, it alone enjoys $50 million in annual revenue, and the broader lobby is “as large and powerful” as the NRA.

Taxpayers also fund the industry: $11.6 million was allocated over three years in the 2024/25 budget to support duck and quail shooting, and it is estimated damage caused by feral deer, protected for hunters, will amount to billions of dollars over the coming decades.

Lobbying and promotion are behind a current “firearms flood” that’s threatening public safety, the research suggests. Lead researcher Rod Campbell says there are now more guns in Australia “than at any point in history, including before the Port Arthur massacre”. The SIFA dismisses the research as “misinformation”.

In a March 17 memo, a Labor delegate warned ministers that “if this hunting lobby hold over the Victorian branch of the party and its factions … were to become public knowledge in the approach to the November 2026 state election, it would not bode well for Labor’s credibility”.

The memo continues: “The extent to which these unions have come under the influence of the gun and hunting lobbies is also not yet widely understood”, as they operate “within Labor factions, particularly the Socialist Left”.

This is Premier Jacinta Allan’s factional power base, making up critical numbers. Insiders say this explains why the premier rejected police and Labor calls for a cap on gun ownership after the Bondi massacre. Holding a press event at Trelly’s Outdoor hunting supplies shop in her Bendigo East electorate late last month, Allan refused to cap the number of guns a Victorian can own.

She has made other unpopular but gun-friendly captain’s calls. She has ignored scientific recommendations and instead protected feral deer for game hunters, rejected a state inquiry recommendation to ban native duck shooting, and broken Labor promises of reclassifying forests as national parks.

The Saturday Paper asked the premier’s department whether Allan’s captain’s calls were due to gun lobby pressure within the Socialist Left faction. A government spokesperson responded: “We’re focused on doing what matters to Victorians, like helping with the cost of living, delivering better and free health care, the best education and keeping Victorians safe. We’re strengthening Victoria’s firearm laws to better target dangerous offenders, while ensuring legitimate firearm owners who follow the rules are not unfairly impacted. Duck hunting is a legitimate activity and it supports regional communities and economies.”

Asked whether the proposed super-agency Outdoor Recreation Victoria had been pushed by the hunting lobby, the spokesperson said: “Outdoor Recreation Victoria’s role is to promote safe, responsible and sustainable outdoor recreation, including legal game hunting.”

Witnesses confirm Breier’s accounts of enduring “hysterical woman” tropes when her motions support environment protections. By their accounts, she was aggressively heckled, “howled down” and intimidated during this May’s state Labor conference. Two delegates name a Labor figure who, they say, had been tasked by a committee with advocating its environmental policy but instead humiliated and blocked Breier when she put forward the very policy motions the committee advocated.

Major trade unions and key figures within government agencies were invited to respond to allegations in this article.

Breier says whatever the outcome of her court applications, she “won’t be silenced”.

“I will be attacked for coming out of the tent,” she says, “but I am being slaughtered inside the tent. I never signed up to the Shooters and Fishers Party, which is what Victorian Labor has become.”

Katherine Wilson is a journalist and author.
